subject: Efficient way to compute distance in rstan

messages.author: 82e8106f84fe4fab
messages.subject: Efficient way to compute distance in rstan
parts:
Hi everyone,

I am trying to generate all combinations of 2 for the elements of each column of a matrix and finding the squared difference between them. Please find below an implementation of what I am trying to do. For example, 
[[1,2],[2,4],[3,6]] will give [[(1-2)^2,(2-4)^2],[(1-3)^2,(2-6)^2],[(2-3)^2,(4-6)^2]] = [[1,4],[4,16],[1,4]]

Does anyone know a more efficient way to do this in rstan?

#############################################
# R Code
# example of matrix for which combinations is to be generated for each column
mat <- matrix(
  c(1,2,3,2,4,6),
  nrow=3,
  ncol=2)
# use combn function to generate all combinations of all elements
# The aim is to pass index into stan and use stan to generate the combinations
index <- combn(nrow(m),m=2) 
dat <- list(mat=mat,index=index,n=ncol(index),numRow=nrow(mat),numCol=ncol(mat)...)

#############################################
# Stan Code

functions {
  matrix get_dist(matrix m, int[,] idx, int n){
    matrix[n,cols(m)] output;
    for(i in 1:cols(m)){
      for(j in 1:n){
        output[j,i] <- (m[idx[1,j],i]-m[idx[2,j],i])^2;
      }
    }
    return output;
  }
}

data {
  int n;
  int numRow;
  int numCol;
  matrix[numRow,numCol] mat;
  int index[2,n];
}

transformed data {
  matrix[n,numCol] combn;
  combn <- get_dist(mat,index,n)
  print(combn);
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Efficient way to compute distance in rstan
parts:
I think that's actually squared distance, not distance. If
you just want distance, you can use the built-in hypot(x, y)
function. Otherwise, there's not going to be a more efficient
way to do this. I'd suggest using square(x - y) instead of
(x - y)^2, but that's a minor savings given that I think our
pow(x-y, 2) checks for a 2 and reduces to square() call.

- Bob
